_what: The five elements of T10's published P3 client contract (T25 spec §2.3). `served` is the DECLARATION; the run COMPUTES the same field by driving each element against the real relay over a real socket, and the coverage scenario asserts the two sets are EQUAL.
_why_equality: Equality, never 'at most' and never 'at least'. An element that starts being served has to move this file, and an element that stops being served goes red without one. A register that only forbade regressions would let the relay quietly grow a behaviour nobody reviewed; one that only forbade additions would let it lose one.
_why_parts: Two of the five elements are CONJUNCTIONS, and a conjunction that publishes only its result cannot tell which half moved — worse, a mutation that flips one conjunct while the AND stays false is INVISIBLE to an equality over `served` alone. `parts` is declared question by question and compared question by question. `not-reached` is a third value on purpose: a question the run could not ask is recorded as unasked, never as answered `false`.
_mutation: flip any `served` value and the coverage scenario goes red naming the element and quoting what the client observed. Flip any `parts` value and the part-equality scenario goes red naming the element AND the part. Delete an element and the `five contract elements are examined` assertion goes red.
_the_client_became_conforming_again: 2026-08-13. foundry main 55f6359d landed the relay's AUTH MIDDLE and this fixture stopped being a conforming client: three elements went red — `the conforming client is admitted`, `version-negotiation` and `host-binding-before-upgrade` — and every one of them was the relay being right. The relay now requires five more request headers (`x-foundry-identity-key`, `x-foundry-location-id`, `x-foundry-connect-nonce`, `x-foundry-connect-timestamp`, `x-foundry-connect-proof`), a BIP-340 Schnorr proof over secp256k1 covering the seven canonical fields of `identity::connect_body` under `fx/relay/connect/v1`, and — LAST, so the door is not an oracle for `is this key a member here` — enrolment against a projection of the community's SIGNED log. THE THREE FAILURES COLLAPSED INTO ONE REPAIR: a conforming client. What that cost is recorded rather than absorbed. (1) `communityPid` can no longer be a literal: `membership::fold` binds entry zero of `communities/<pid>.log` to the pid the deployment bound the host to, so the community IS its founding key and the fixture generates one. (2) The fixture writes a real signed membership log — a `Found` by the community key and an `Admit` of the client's key — because a deployment that binds a host to a community it holds no log for refuses everybody. (3) The client needed BIP-340 Schnorr over secp256k1, which this package does not have in any form: CryptoKit ships P-256 and Curve25519, swift-crypto has no secp256k1, and `grep -rn secp256k1 Sources Tests` was empty. It is IMPLEMENTED IN THIS TARGET rather than added as a package dependency — see `Secp256k1Schnorr.swift` for the three reasons, of which the load-bearing one is that this target's whole discipline is a client that does not agree with the relay by construction. It was validated against a golden vector produced by `foundry_signing` + `k256` itself (identical canonical encoding, identical pre-image, identical 64 signature bytes) and against BIP-340's published public keys, and the relay is the standing oracle: a wrong signature is a 403 indistinguishable from every other 403.
_mutations_run_2026_08_13: THREE MUTATIONS, ALL KILLED, all run against the real relay rather than reasoned about. (M1) The unbound-host drive pointed at an address refused by a DIFFERENT conjunct — an all-whitespace host, which the relay refuses at the guard ABOVE the lookup: the two WIRE questions stayed `met` (403, never upgraded) and only `unbound-host-refused-at-the-binding` went `unmet`, reporting `the door recorded no refusal against `   ` at all`. That is the whole case for the third question in one run: the wire cannot tell those two refusals apart and the seam can. (M2) The client signed a version the exchange did not produce (`version + 1`): the conforming-client scenario went red and `version-negotiation` reported EXACTLY the pre-repair baseline — `offered 1 and the reply named no version at all (the reply's headers were [Connection, Content-Length])` — which is what makes the `version` field of the connect body demonstrably load-bearing rather than copied out of a struct. (M3) The community's signed log admitted a different key: `0 admission(s) were recorded against bound.example`, so the enrolment leg is real and the log is not decoration.
_provenance: every `served` value below was set from a run, not from reading the relay's source. Two of them contradicted the author's prediction before the run: `auth-timeout` was predicted NOT served and is served (crates/foundry-relay/src/serve.rs:380-381 really does set a socket read timeout from the deployed key), and that correction is the reason this file records observations rather than expectations.

elements.name: the (normalized_host || negotiated_version) prologue, bound into the handshake
elements.observed: the connect wire refused a prologue in both encodings (2 of 2), which is what the design requires of it; after HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols the relay was handed a 32-byte opening message and closed the connection without sending one handshake byte, so there is no step-3 handshake for a prologue to be mixed into and the binding differential was NOT REACHED
elements.owner: T10 — this is the relay's obligation, not this track's. T25 drives it and reports; it does not implement it.
elements._respecified: 2026-08-13. THIS ELEMENT WAS MIS-SPECIFIED AND THE PREVIOUS ROW RECORDED A FALSE REASON. It drove the element by sending `(boundHost || "p3")` ahead of the request head and recorded the relay's 403 as `it reads a request line, not a prologue` — a sentence that reads as a relay defect and is not one. THE DESIGN SAYS THE DRIVER WAS WRONG, on three independent counts: (1) `design/03-protocols.md` P3 orders the protocol as `1. TCP/TLS + tenant bind BEFORE the upgrade -> 2. version negotiation -> 3. mutual handshake (Noise-XX) with prologue = (normalized_host || negotiated_version)`, with the per-connection state machine `tcp-open -> tenant-bound -> version-negotiated -> handshaking`; the prologue is step 3 and the old drive put it two states early. (2) T10 spec §5.1 RESOLVES the connect wire — the version offer rides `the same pre-upgrade request that carries the host` and the relay `echoes the negotiated version in the upgrade acceptance, and binds it into the prologue` — so the bytes at connect are an HTTP head and a 101, and a relay that accepted a prologue-shaped prefix ahead of that head would be speaking a protocol no document designs. (3) A NOISE PROLOGUE IS NEVER TRANSMITTED, and this repository's own primitive is the proof: `Sources/FoundryXKit/NoiseXX.swift:209-211` and `:317-319` take `prologue: Data` and `mixHash` it — it is an input to the transcript hash both peers must already hold. That is precisely the property 03-protocols claims for it (`a handshake transcript completed for community A's host cannot be replayed against community B, because the prologue disagrees`), and a prologue put on the wire would give no such property, because the replaying peer would send the same bytes. The old drive's VALUE was wrong too: it concatenated the literal `p3`, and `P3` is the protocol's ordinal name (03-protocols P1..P9) while T10 §2.3 pins a version as an unsigned integer 1..=65535. CORRECTED 2026-08-13 (fourth lane): COUNT (3) ABOVE OVERSTATES ITS CASE AND THIS PROGRAM HAD ALREADY WITHDRAWN THE OVERSTATEMENT BEFORE THIS FILE REPEATED IT. `rungs-run.md` records `A claim from the first draft of this ruling, WITHDRAWN` — the Noise framework expressly permits a prologue to carry negotiation data that WAS transmitted, and the replay property comes from both parties mixing the SAME context with the responder DERIVING host and version, not from the bytes being secret or unsent. A gpt-5.6-sol review found the withdrawn claim still standing here and in `ContractElements.swift`. The RULING IS UNCHANGED and does not rest on it: counts (1) and (2) are untouched, and what survives of (3) — the prologue is MIXED into the transcript hash, not sent as a prefix ahead of the request head — is what `NoiseXX.swift:209-211/:317-319` actually does and is all the ruling ever needed. Recorded rather than quietly edited, because this register has now collected the same withdrawn argument twice.
elements._blocked_on: T10 PHASE-4 task 4.2 (`bind the version into the prologue and the transcript`), itself blocked on T06's signing API, and T10 PHASE-10 (the published contract with a golden vector per element) — both recorded as blocked in foundry `evidence/t10/registers/blocked-tasks.toml`. NO CHANGE TO THIS TARGET CAN SERVE THIS ELEMENT: there is no step-3 handshake in `crates/foundry-relay` at all (`serve.rs` ends at the 101 and says so: `Step 1 is the PRE-upgrade exchange. It stops here on purpose`). What this target owes is a true observation and a drive that flips the day the relay grows one. A SECOND BLOCKER, ON THIS SIDE OF THE WIRE, RECORDED FOR THE FIRST TIME 2026-08-13: EVEN IF THE RELAY GREW STEP 3 TOMORROW, THIS CLIENT WOULD BIND NOTHING. Both production consumers construct their initiator with the DEFAULT EMPTY prologue — `Sources/FoundryXKit/RelayTransport.swift:100` and `Sources/FoundryXKit/DoorConnection.swift:281` both call `NoiseXXInitiator(staticPrivate:)` and omit the argument, so `prologue: Data = Data()` applies. The element is therefore blocked on TWO builds, not one, and only one of them is T10's. It is NOT repaired here: `grep -rni prologue --include='*.rs' crates/` in foundry is 0 at `afaba943`, so a non-empty prologue on the Swift side alone would break the live door handshake — this is a change that lands with its counterpart or not at all.
elements._still_owed_by_the_contract: the golden vector. T10 A13 requires `prologue bytes for a fixed host+version` that a contract-only client reproduces byte-for-byte. No document pins the byte encoding of the `||`, so this run asserts nothing about the encoding and drives part 1 with BOTH plausible ones (decimal-ASCII and u16 big-endian) rather than picking one and calling it the contract. AND, RECORDED 2026-08-13 SO THE PHRASE `what is missing is now a SUBJECT rather than an ORACLE` IS NOT READ AS MORE THAN IT SAYS: when the subject arrives, this target still has no live differential to drive. `ContractElements.prologue` deliberately THROWS at that moment and names what must be built. An oracle for the property and an adapter to a real peer are two different things, and only the first exists.
elements._the_oracle_and_what_it_is_not: 2026-08-13. `prologue-binding-differential` has read `not-reached` at every measurement, and until now that phrase was doing two jobs: NOTHING ANSWERED, and NOBODY KNEW HOW TO ASK. Only the first is true of the world. The question is now EXECUTED and mutation-graded, in the hermetic target, at `features/prologue-binding.feature` (6 scenarios, run by `swift test --filter PrologueBindingFeatureTests`, which asserts its own EXECUTED count): two peers that mix the same `(host || version)` complete and carry traffic both ways; peers that disagree about the host, about the version, or by ONE BYTE, cannot complete, and neither is given transport keys. SIX MUTATIONS, ALL KILLED: M1 initiator-only stops mixing (4 of 6 red), M2 BOTH peers stop mixing — which is what `the prologue is not load-bearing` means — (3 red, and the matched run stays green as the failability control), M3 responder-only (4 red), M4 the driver's own oracle given identical bindings (1 red, exactly the target scenario), M5 and M6 the two stimulus scenarios (1 red each). THIS DOES NOT SERVE THE ELEMENT AND MUST NEVER BE READ AS SERVING IT. `served` stays false and the part verdicts are unchanged. The peers are this repository's own; the relay does not use them; the element's owner is T10. THE ANALOGY TO `version-negotiation`'s in-process grading DOES NOT HOLD and is recorded as refused: that table lives INSIDE the relay, which is the subject, and `NoiseXXInitiator` does not — named by a gpt-5.6-sol review. What changed is that what is missing is now a SUBJECT rather than an ORACLE. NOT CLAIMED, by name: the SERIALIZATION of the `||` is still unpinned by any document, so no scenario here asserts a byte encoding, and T10 A13's golden vector is still owed.
elements._part2_drive_repaired: 2026-08-13. Part 2's probe used to write the tenancy bytes themselves after the `101` and wait to be spoken to. Against today's relay that is indistinguishable from any other stimulus — it closes the socket either way — so the verdict `unmet` is unchanged and the served count does not move. Against a relay that GREW step 3 the two are not the same: a peer speaking Noise-XX waits for an OPENING MESSAGE and cannot read 15 bytes of bare tenancy as one, so the old probe would have gone on reporting `unmet` at a relay that had implemented the whole of step 3 — and this row's own promise that the drive `flips the day the relay grows one` was FALSE. Predicted by a gpt-5.6-sol review, then MEASURED both ways against a correctly speaking peer (`prologue-binding.feature`, the last two scenarios: bare tenancy is unreadable as an opening; a 32-byte opening is answered) and graded by M5/M6. The probe now sends a 32-byte opening — raw bytes, not a FoundryXKit transport type, for the same reason `P3Client` speaks raw bytes at all.
elements._route_1_was_measured_not_argued: 2026-08-13, EIGHTH LANE. The standing framing of this element — `the oracle works but sits OUTSIDE the conformance target, SO served stays false` — asserts a CAUSE, and it is FALSE. `served` is computed in `ContractElements.swift` `prologue(...)` from three drives against the relay's socket; which test target the oracle lives in is not an input to any of them. The counterfactual worktree was discarded; nothing from it is landed.
elements._the_two_subjects_argument_was_unsound: 2026-08-13, EIGHTH LANE, AND IT IS A CORRECTION OF THIS PROGRAM'S OWN RULING. The seventh lane refused route 1 partly because admitting the oracle `would mix TWO SUBJECTS inside one target whose reported metric is conformance to the relay's contract`. That premise is not true of this target as it stands. `Tests/FoundryXConformanceTests/DoorFixture.swift:56` constructs a `NoiseXXResponder` — FoundryXKit's own responder — IN THIS PROCESS and completes a real msg1/msg2/msg3 handshake against FoundryXKit's own initiator, because P1's observable is whether the client proceeds against a real counterpart. REPAIRED, AND THE REPAIR IS A COUNT, NOT A SENTENCE: `ConformancePeerCensus` now enumerates the construction sites of FoundryXKit's handshake peer types in this target's own sources and the run asserts TWO numbers — one site in the target (P1's door) and ZERO in the sources that drive the five contract elements. elements._unserved_reason_is_reported_and_is_not_: 2026-08-13. The run now prints, for every unserved element, WHY — `CONFORMANCE: UNSERVED-REASON — prologue-bytes: the subject was asked and did not do it — post-upgrade-handshake-exists; never asked, because the above is unmet: prologue-binding-differential`. The wording is deliberately `answered no` / `never asked` rather than `the subject did not answer`: the relay DID answer the existence question, by closing the socket inside a measured window, and it is the differential that was never put to it — collapsing those into one adjective is how a reader ends up believing the relay went silent on a question it in fact refused. It is strictly OUTSIDE `served`, outside the five elements, and outside the part comparison: it is computed from the same drive and changes no verdict. Its purpose is that a reader can tell `the relay refused` from `the relay has no such phase` without reading the driver, and that `not-reached` cannot become a hiding place. Every unasked question must NAME its blockers, each named blocker must be a real question of the same element, and each must have been answered `unmet` — `there is some other unmet question` was the first draft of this rule and it is too weak, because for this element the connect-wire question would have satisfied it while the differential quietly went unasked behind a failure it never depended on. A gpt-5.6-sol review named that hole before it landed. The number of `not-reached` questions is itself declared, so one that stops being recorded unasked is not a smaller pass. IT DOES NOT MOVE THIS ELEMENT ONE STEP TOWARDS SERVED. elements.name: version negotiation as a wire exchange, not an asserted field
elements.observed: offered 1 and the reply named X-Foundry-Protocol-Version: 1; a legal offer of 65535 the relay does not speak answered HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden; an absent offer answered HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden — a real exchange since foundry 7f6ed530 (feat(t10): version negotiation the relay actually reads, 2026-08-12), and since 55f6359d an echo only a CONFORMING client can reach at all
elements._the_echo_now_costs_a_proof: 2026-08-13. This element WENT RED against foundry main 55f6359d — `offered 1 and the reply named no version at all (the reply's headers were [Connection, Content-Length])` — and the relay was right. The auth middle refuses a client that cannot prove which key is on the connection, and A REFUSAL CARRIES NO `X-Foundry-Protocol-Version`: negotiation runs BEFORE the auth middle and the echo is written only into the `101` (`serve.rs`: the echo line is part of the upgrade response and nothing else). So there is no repair on the reporting side of this element — no header to look for on a 403, and asking the relay to echo on a refusal would leak which phase the connection reached, which is the whole point of one byte-identical denial. The element is served the only way it can be: by making the client CONFORMING — five signed connect-frame headers over a BIP-340 proof, and a community membership log the relay can fold the client's key out of — and observing the echo on the upgrade it then gets. THE TWO REFUSAL LEGS ARE UNCHANGED AND STILL PROVE THE RELAY READ THE OFFER: both `65535` and an absent offer are refused BEFORE the auth middle runs, so neither owes its 403 to the new gate.
elements._strengthened: 2026-08-13. The previous drive made ONE offer, accepted any reply header whose name merely CONTAINED `version`, and asserted nothing about an offer the relay cannot meet — so a relay that stamped a constant header on every reply would have passed it, which is the exact defect the element exists to detect. It now asserts the echoed VALUE is a member of what was offered, and drives both refusal directions. The refusal direction is what proves the relay READ the offer rather than decorated the reply. A SECOND DEFECT IN THAT SAME STRENGTHENING, found by the same review and killed: the reply was matched on any LINE containing the word `version`, so a relay that shipped a build stamp — `X-Build-Version: 1` — satisfied the element while never naming a protocol version. Measured both ways against a relay mutated to do exactly that: with the old matcher rc=0 and served (THE MUTATION SURVIVED); with the matcher reading the header NAME and requiring it to mean a negotiated protocol version, rc=1 and `the reply named no version at all (the reply's headers were [Upgrade, Connection, X-Build-Version, X-Foundry-Session-Token])`.
elements._what_this_element_CANNOT_see: TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVE IT, BOTH MEASURED, BOTH WITH ONE ARITHMETIC CAUSE. (M6) Mutating `negotiation::select` from `.max()` to `.min()` in the real relay, rebuilding, re-running this suite: rc=0, still served — the ORDERING ORACLE T10 2.3 pins (`max(offer intersect supported)`) is invisible from outside. (M8) Replacing the echoed selection with the LITERAL CONSTANT `1`: rc=0, still served — 'the relay echoes what it selected' and 'the relay echoes 1' are the same observation here. The cause of both is that the relay's SUPPORTED set has exactly one member (1), so max and min agree on every offer and the only successful offer IS 1. NO change to a client outside the relay can distinguish them while that holds; the second one dies the day SUPPORTED gains a member, and this row should be re-measured then. Both rules are graded where they are observable — the relay's own in-process vector table (T10 A9). M8 was named by a gpt-5.6-sol review of this file's own change and then run; it was a prediction that turned out true, not a limitation anybody had noticed from the inside.

elements.name: host-bound tenancy established before the socket upgrades
elements.observed: the bound address answered HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols; nobody.example answered HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden and never upgraded; 4 admission(s) were recorded against bound.example bound to this deployment's community, and the door recorded 2 refusal(s) against nobody.example, deciding on unmapped-host — read from the door's own seam, because all 18 refusal causes write identical bytes and the wire cannot tell them apart
elements._became_a_conjunction: 2026-08-13. This element was ONE question until foundry's relay landed its auth middle (N1 roster resolution, N3 signed host-bound proof, N4 typed session context; foundry main 55f6359d), and the change is a REPAIR of lost discrimination, not a strengthening for its own sake. The old drive was two wire observations — the bound address upgrades, the unbound one is refused and never upgrades — and the second of them stopped meaning anything: `serve::RefusalCause::ALL` is now EIGHTEEN causes and every one writes the same `REFUSAL_RESPONSE` bytes, so `nobody.example answered 403` is satisfied by a relay that refused for a reason with nothing to do with host binding. THE ONE REFUSAL IS CORRECT AND THIS TARGET DOES NOT ASK FOR IT TO BE WEAKENED: per-cause bytes are exactly what would let an unauthenticated caller map the deployment. The discrimination is recovered where the relay put it — the door's CQRS seam log (`seam/auth.log` inside the deployment directory, `admit-connection` on the command side and `resolve-principal` on the query side), which records the normalized host the relay DERIVED and the conjunct that decided. The third question requires an `accept` recorded against the bound host AND this deployment's community, and requires EVERY refusal recorded against the unbound host to name `unmapped-host` — i.e. the relay reached tenancy resolution and refused THERE, not at a guard above it and not at identity or enrolment below it.
elements._why_not_the_lookup_counter: 2026-08-13. `Serving::resolver_lookups_attempted()` is the accessor the relay grew for `the guard runs BEFORE the lookup`, and it is NOT what this element reads, for two independent reasons. (1) It is unreachable: it is an in-process accessor on a `Serving` handle, this harness holds a spawned PROCESS, and no HTTP route serves it — deliberately, for the same reason no route serves the per-cause counters. (2) It would answer a different question. `tenancy::resolve_binding` records the lookup FIRST, `before anything can return early`, so a BOUND and an UNBOUND host both move it; the only thing that leaves it still is a host refused by the guard ABOVE the lookup, which is the empty-host case, and that is `generic-rejections`' stimulus rather than this element's. Recorded because the counter is the obvious thing to reach for here and it is the wrong instrument.

elements.name: the bounded AUTH_TIMEOUT, client-observable
elements.observed: said nothing at all and the relay closed the connection within a window that TRACKS the number it was deployed with. The tracking half is load-bearing: a relay that answered instantly would satisfy 'answered within the bound' while having never heard of the bound.

elements.name: byte-identical generic rejections
elements.observed: 8 externally reachable refusal STIMULI produced 1 distinct reply on the wire, all HTTP/1.1 403. STIMULI, not in-process causes: `an empty address` and `an address of nothing but spaces` both reach the relay's single EmptyHost cause, so the 8 stimuli cover 7 distinct RefusalCause variants — a number a client outside the relay cannot see, and which the earlier wording `8 distinct causes` wrongly asserted.
elements.owner: T10 — served on the byte-identity component only. T10's own spec §2.2 defines the rejection as an OBSERVATION TUPLE (bytes, phase at close, status/close code, whether anything preceded the close, timing class) partitioned into a pre-upgrade cohort P and a post-upgrade cohort H. Every cause this client can reach from outside today is cohort P, so cohort H and the non-byte components of the tuple are UNCOVERED here and are named as such rather than counted.
elements._widened: 2026-08-13, from 6 causes to 8. D7's differential names wrong-tenant / unknown-host / BAD-VERSION / timeout, and bad-version was unreachable for as long as negotiation was a constant. It is reachable now, in both of its shapes — an offer that cannot be read (the relay's MalformedOffer) and a legal offer with no common member (NoCommonVersion) — and both are driven here and required to be indistinguishable from `nobody bound that address`. The timeout remains excluded by name (T10 spec §5.2), so the differential is 8 pre-upgrade causes, not D7's four-case tuple.
